species/anomalocaris.title: Anomalocaris
species/anomalocaris.summary: Anomalocaris was a large swimming Cambrian animal with spiny grasping appendages, a round mouth ringed by plates, and large compound eyes. It lived about 515 to 505 million years ago, is known from Canada and Australia, and is a stem-group relative of arthropods.
facts: Anomalocaris is securely known from the Burgess Shale of British Columbia (about 505 million years old) and the Emu Bay Shale of South Australia (about 515). Chinese fossils once assigned to it have mostly been moved to other genera.

Its appendages were described in 1892 as a crustacean tail, its mouth as a jellyfish, and its body as a sea cucumber. Harry Whittington and Derek Briggs showed in 1985 that they belonged to one animal.
Complete Burgess specimens are about 20 to 25 cm long. Estimates of 35 to 50 cm include appendages and tail, and a claim of about 1 m rests on fragments.
Compound eyes from the Emu Bay Shale, up to 3 cm long, preserve at least 16,000 lenses, comparable to the sharpest-sighted living arthropods.
The mouth looks too weak to crush trilobite shells, and studies propose suction feeding or soft prey. Whether it was the top predator of its seas is debated.
species/anomalocaris.context: Anomalocaris lived in the Cambrian Period, a signature animal of the Cambrian Explosion, sharing seas with Trilobites, Hallucigenia, and Pikaia. Its sites include the Burgess Shale, the Emu Bay Shale, and Chengjiang Fossil Site. See Earth Systems and Life and Science.
species/anomalocaris.observer: The Observer notes that Anomalocaris was first assembled from three fossils believed to be three animals, and that the apex predator of popular pictures depends on how its mouth is read. It is one of many body plans that arose and vanished in the Cambrian, when nothing marked in advance which would leave descendants. The reading would weaken if radiodonts were shown to be ancestral to a living animal group.
questions: What did Anomalocaris eat?
How many valid species does the genus include?

species/archaea.title: Archaea
species/archaea.summary: Archaea are single-celled organisms without a nucleus that form one of the three domains of life, with Bacteria and eukaryotes. Recognized as separate only in 1977, they may date to about 3.5 billion years ago, though no fossil archaeon has been identified with confidence.
facts: In 1977 Carl Woese and George Fox used ribosomal RNA sequences to show that methane-producing microbes were as distinct from bacteria as from eukaryotes. In 1990 the three domains were named Bacteria, Archaea, and Eucarya.

Archaea were first known from hot springs, salt lakes, and methane-rich mud, but they also live in soils, deep sediments, and the open ocean, where in one Pacific study they made up about 39 percent of the smallest plankton at depth.

The earliest evidence is indirect. Methane in Australian rocks about 3.5 billion years old was read in 2006 as microbial, but nonliving processes can give similar isotope values. Molecular clocks range from 3.5 to 4.1 billion years, and are also disputed.

Asgard archaea, first found in 2015, carry genes for proteins otherwise known only in eukaryotes. Some researchers therefore place eukaryotes inside Archaea, which would leave two primary domains, not three.
No archaeon is established as a human pathogen.
species/archaea.context: Archaea trace to the Last Universal Common Ancestor and the Origin of Life, and belong to the Archean Eon. Their relatives gave rise to eukaryotic cells; see Origin of Eukaryotes. Compare the bacterial Cyanobacteria. See Earth Systems and Life and Science.
species/archaea.observer: The Observer notes that a third branch of life sat unrecognized in hot springs and salt lakes until sequence comparison revealed it in 1977, and that the species' own cells possibly descend from a merger involving an archaeon. The Observer takes it that categories are set by the tools available. The reading would weaken if eukaryotes proved not to have archaeal ancestry.
questions: When did archaea first appear?
Which Asgard lineage is closest to eukaryotes?

species/archaeopteryx.title: Archaeopteryx
species/archaeopteryx.summary: Archaeopteryx was a feathered, winged dinosaur about the size of a raven, known from Late Jurassic limestone in Bavaria, Germany, about 150 million years old.
facts: Fossils come from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany.
It combined bird-like features, such as feathers and wings, with reptile-like ones, including teeth, clawed fingers, and a long bony tail.
The first skeleton was found in 1861, two years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species, and was quickly cited as a transitional form.
Feathered non-avian dinosaurs found in China from the 1990s onward strengthened the link between birds and theropod dinosaurs.
Birds are the living descendants of theropod dinosaurs.
species/archaeopteryx.context: Archaeopteryx documents the origin of birds within the Dinosaurs; birds were the dinosaur lineage that survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction. It was an early prop for the evolutionary ideas of Charles Darwin. Archaeopteryx sits in the Mesozoic Era and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
species/archaeopteryx.observer: The Observer notes that the dinosaurs did not fully end; they are still on every continent as birds. The species that studies extinctions overhead lives among survivors of one of them.
questions: Was Archaeopteryx capable of powered flight or only gliding?

species/australopithecus-afarensis.title: Australopithecus afarensis
species/australopithecus-afarensis.summary: Australopithecus afarensis was an early hominin that lived in East Africa about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago and walked upright, and is best known from the fossil 'Lucy'.
facts: 'Lucy' was found in Hadar, Ethiopia, in 1974 and is about 3.2 million years old.
Footprints at Laetoli, Tanzania (about 3.66 million years old), record upright walking.
It had a small brain (estimates range from about 380 to 550 cubic centimeters) and long arms adapted to climbing.
It is often considered close to the ancestry of the genus Homo.
species/australopithecus-afarensis.context: The species follows the Divergence of the Hominin Lineage and precedes Homo habilis.
species/australopithecus-afarensis.observer: The Observer notes that upright walking came long before big brains. The species' most distinctive trait, a large brain, was a late addition to a lineage that had been walking for millions of years.
questions: Was A. afarensis a direct ancestor of Homo?

species/barley.title: Barley
species/barley.summary: Barley is a cereal grass domesticated in the Fertile Crescent from around 9000 BCE, one of the earliest crops farmed by humans and, in ancient Mesopotamia, a staple used as food, drink and even a standard of value.
facts: Barley was domesticated from wild barley in the Fertile Crescent, with early domesticated forms recorded in the Jarmo region of modern Iraq from about 9000 to 7000 BCE; grinding stones with starch traces from wild barley at Ohalo II, near the Sea of Galilee, show it was eaten well before domestication, by about 23,000 BCE.
Domestication produced grain heads that hold together instead of shattering, making the plant far easier to harvest but dependent on deliberate replanting.
Barley was likely among the first grains brewed into beer, one of the earliest alcoholic drinks made by Neolithic farmers.

In Mesopotamia, barley served as a de facto currency, with the shekel functioning as a standard unit of its weight, and cuneiform records from around 2350 BCE, under the ruler Urukagina, describe monthly barley rations issued to adults.

By about 2000 BCE barley had spread across Eurasia, reaching Finland by about 4200 BCE, the Indus civilization region between roughly 5,700 and 3,300 years ago, and the Korean peninsula by about 1500 to 850 BCE.

Global production reached about 146 million tonnes in 2023, the fourth largest cereal harvest after maize, rice and wheat; about 70 percent goes to animal feed and about 30 percent to malting for beer and whisky.
species/barley.context: Barley was domesticated alongside Wheat as one of the founding crops of The Agricultural Revolution in the Fertile Crescent, and it underwrote the economies of early Mesopotamian cities such as Ur and, later, Babylon. It sits in the Neolithic and the region Mesopotamia, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Kinship and Society.
species/barley.observer: The Observer notes that a grain used as both food and a unit of account collapses two functions that many later societies kept separate, food and money, and that Mesopotamian rationing records turn barley into a record of a kin-lattice's obligations, who was owed what and by whom. Brewing barley into beer is one of the oldest recorded transformations of a raw crop into a socially significant product, tying farming to gathering and celebration. The reading would weaken if barley's early monetary role proves to have been more local and limited than the shekel-based accounts suggest.
questions: How standard was barley's role as a unit of value across different Mesopotamian cities and periods?
How soon after domestication did brewing become widespread, as opposed to barley being eaten mainly as porridge or bread?

species/black-rat.title: Black Rat
species/black-rat.summary: The black rat (Rattus rattus) is a rodent native to South Asia and Southeast Asia that became one of the most widespread commensals of humans, spreading with trade and shipping across Eurasia and later the world, and acting as a major vector of plague.
facts: Genetic studies find well-differentiated black rat lineages native to South Asia, the Himalayan region and Indochina, with diversification beginning long before human involvement; exactly when black rats first became commensal with people in that homeland is not precisely dated.

Black rats spread out of South Asia along trade routes to the Near East and Egypt in antiquity, and documented Roman-era shipping and trade carried them across the Mediterranean and into the wider Roman Empire, reaching as far as Britain by about the 1st century CE.
As a commensal species, the black rat thrives in and around human granaries, ships and settlements, feeding on stored grain and waste, which let it travel wherever people and cargo moved.

Fleas carried on black rats are considered a major vector of Yersinia pestis, the bacterium behind the Plague of Justinian and the Black Death, though the disease's spread beyond rat-infested areas suggests other means of transmission, including human fleas and lice, also mattered.

The black rat was later displaced from much of Europe and North America by the larger brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), which spread from Asia in the 18th century, though black rats remain widespread in warmer regions and on many islands.

As an invasive species on islands without native rodents, black rats have caused the extinction or decline of ground-nesting birds and other native species, a continuing ecological effect of their spread.
species/black-rat.context: The black rat traveled the Opening of the Silk Roads and Mediterranean shipping lanes of the Romans, and its fleas are implicated in the transmission of the Black Death. Black Rat sits in Classical Antiquity (its documented Roman-era spread) and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Trade and Economy.
species/black-rat.observer: The Observer offers a reading, not a fact: the black rat shows that an exchange-web built for grain and cloth can carry unintended passengers, so that trade and sanctioned harm are connected through a rodent that neither side of any transaction intended to move. Wherever ships and granaries created new habitat, this one species followed without domestication, a hitchhiker riding humanity's own tool-lineage of storage and transport. The reading would weaken if genetic dating eventually shows the rat's major dispersals tracking climate and rodent competition more than human shipping.
questions: When did black rats first become commensal with people in South Asia, and how long before their Old World spread?
How much of the Black Death's transmission depended on black rats specifically, as against human ectoparasites?

species/cacao.title: Cacao
species/cacao.summary: Cacao, the source of chocolate, was first domesticated in the Amazon basin of South America by at least 3300 BCE and later became a ritual drink and currency in Mesoamerica before Spanish traders carried it to Europe in the 16th century.
facts: Cacao's native range is the Amazon rainforest, and genetic and archaeological evidence places its earliest domestication at the Santa Ana-La Florida site in present-day Ecuador, by the Mayo-Chinchipe culture, at least 5,300 years ago, before it reached Mesoamerica.

Chemical residue on pottery from Puerto Escondido, Honduras, shows cacao products were being consumed there between about 1500 and 1400 BCE, with the sweet pulp around the beans likely valued before the beans themselves.

Across Mesoamerica before the Spanish conquest, cacao beans served as a currency for everyday purchases, and Olmec and Maya elites drank cacao in spiritual ceremonies; a Spanish chronicler recorded that the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II drank only chocolate, reportedly consuming dozens of servings a day from a golden goblet.

Spanish traders introduced chocolate to Europe, and it became a popular drink there by the mid-17th century; the Spanish also spread cacao cultivation to their colonies in the West Indies and the Philippines.

Ivory Coast and Ghana together grow most of the world's cacao today, and reporting on the industry has documented large-scale child labor: an estimated 2.1 million children were involved in cocoa harvesting in the two countries as of 2017, often exposed to pesticides and hazardous tasks; a 2021 lawsuit against major chocolate companies over forced child labor was dismissed for lack of a traceable link to specific plantations.
Global cacao production reached about 5.8 million tonnes in 2022, with Ivory Coast alone supplying about 38 percent.
species/cacao.context: Cacao was central to the ritual and economic life of the Olmecs, the Maya and the Aztec Empire before Spanish contact, and its spread to Europe and other continents is part of the Columbian Exchange. It sits in the Bronze Age and the region Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
species/cacao.observer: The Observer notes that cacao moved from a South American forest crop to a Mesoamerican meaning-engine, functioning at once as money, medicine and a marker of elite status, and then to a European luxury good stripped of most of that ritual weight and remade as a sweet. Today's cacao economy repeats an old pattern in a new form: a crop grown mainly by smallholders in West Africa supplies a global confectionery industry, and the labor of children within that supply chain is recorded here as harm, whatever the difficulty of tracing it to a specific buyer. The reading would weaken if cacao's currency role in Mesoamerica proves to have been more limited or local than the general accounts suggest.
questions: How did cacao move from its South American origin to becoming culturally central in Mesoamerica, and by what route and over what timescale?
How effective have industry pledges and lawsuits been at reducing child labor in West African cacao production?

species/cassava.title: Cassava
species/cassava.summary: Cassava is a starchy root crop domesticated in south-central Brazil, likely within the last 10,000 years, that requires processing to remove natural toxins and that Portuguese and Spanish traders carried to Africa and Asia in the 16th century, where it became a staple for hundreds of millions of people.
facts: Cassava was domesticated from wild relatives centered in west-central Brazil; the date of domestication is imprecise, likely within the last 10,000 years, and cassava pollen appears in Gulf of Mexico lowland sediment by about 4600 BCE, with the oldest direct evidence of cultivation coming from the Maya site of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador, about 1,400 years old.

Raw cassava contains cyanogenic compounds, linamarin and lotaustralin, that release toxic hydrogen cyanide; bitter varieties can carry up to 1,000 milligrams of cyanide per kilogram of fresh root, and communities developed soaking and fermentation methods, some reducing cyanide content by 85 to 99 percent, to make the crop safe to eat.

Portuguese traders introduced cassava from Brazil to West Africa in the 16th century, and Portuguese and Spanish traders also carried it to their colonies in Goa, Malacca, eastern Indonesia, Timor and the Philippines; it reached East Africa by about 1850 through Arab and European traders.

Cassava is now a primary food staple for an estimated 500 million to 800 million people, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, and it ranks as the tropics' third-largest carbohydrate source after rice and maize, valued for growing on poor soils with little rainfall.
Global cassava production reached about 330 million tonnes in 2022, with Nigeria the largest producer and Thailand the largest exporter of cassava starch.
species/cassava.context: Cassava's domestication belongs to the wider The Agricultural Revolution in the Americas, and its 16th-century spread to Africa and Asia is part of the Columbian Exchange; in West and Central Africa it became a staple food during the era of the Atlantic Slave Trade. It sits in the Neolithic and the region Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Technology.
species/cassava.observer: The Observer notes that cassava is unusual among staple crops in requiring a tool-lineage of processing, soaking or fermenting, before it can be safely eaten, so its adoption in Africa and Asia carried with it a body of practical knowledge as well as the plant itself, an example of an exchange-web moving techniques alongside seeds. Its tolerance of poor soil made it valuable precisely where colonial and later national agricultural systems demanded a reliable staple with little investment, which the Observer reads as an example of a crop's usefulness under stress shaping which regions came to depend on it. The reading would weaken if processing knowledge is shown to have traveled independently of the crop rather than together with it.
questions: How did processing knowledge for detoxifying cassava spread alongside the crop itself in Africa and Asia?
How much do modern reliance on a narrow range of cassava varieties leave current staple supplies vulnerable to disease, as happened with the potato in 19th-century Europe?

species/cattle.title: Cattle
species/cattle.summary: Cattle are large grazing animals domesticated from the wild aurochs in southwestern Asia about 10,500 years ago, and with over 940 million animals today they are among the most numerous and heaviest livestock on Earth.
facts: Domestic cattle descend from the aurochs (Bos primigenius), a wild ox that once ranged across Europe, North Africa and much of Asia; humans hunted aurochs long before domestication, and that older history is outside this note.

Taurine cattle were domesticated about 10,500 years ago in a zone spanning central Anatolia, the Levant and western Iran, and mitochondrial DNA suggests the taurine line may descend from as few as about 80 aurochs tamed in upper Mesopotamia.
A separate domestication on the Indian subcontinent produced the humped zebu cattle.

Cattle are kept for meat, milk and leather and as draft animals that pull carts and farm implements; taurine cattle spread across Europe and temperate Asia and were later carried by Europeans to the Americas and Australia.

More than 940 million cattle lived in the world in 2022, led by India (about 307 million), Brazil (about 194 million) and China (about 102 million); by one estimate they have the largest biomass of any animal species, about 650 million tonnes.
Cattle farming accounts for about 7 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, mostly methane from digestion, and overgrazing has reduced biodiversity in some rangelands.
Cattle are sacred in Hinduism, and slaughter of cows is forbidden by law in several Indian states and in Nepal.
species/cattle.context: Cattle were brought under Animal Domestication alongside Sheep and Goat as part of The Agricultural Revolution in southwestern Asia, and their carrying to the Americas after 1492 belongs to the Columbian Exchange. Cattle sit in the Neolithic and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belong to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Religion and Belief and Earth Systems and Life.
species/cattle.observer: The Observer offers a reading, not a fact: cattle turn grass that humans cannot digest into milk, meat and pulling power, so a herd works as wealth that walks, and in many pastoral societies its size acts as a status-signal and a record of kin-lattice obligations. The same animal is property in one society and sacred in another, so one species carries opposite meaning-engines without changing at all, and its methane now ties a Neolithic partnership to the planet's climate. The reading would weaken if herd size proves to have signaled status in far fewer societies than this account assumes.
questions: How many separate taming events lie behind taurine cattle, and how did zebu and taurine lines mix as herds moved across Asia and Africa?
How did ploughing with cattle change the size of fields and settlements after domestication?

species/chicken.title: Chicken
species/chicken.summary: The chicken descends from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, was carried across the Pacific and the Old World, and is now the most numerous bird on Earth, with more than 26 billion alive in 2023; the timing of its domestication is uncertain.
facts: Chickens descend from the red junglefowl (Gallus gallus), native to Southeast Asia, and still interbreed with it.

Genomic studies estimate that chickens were domesticated about 8,000 years ago in Southeast Asia, but the earliest bones judged probably chicken come from Ban Non Wat in central Thailand, about 3,250 years old, and older claims from China are debated; the date_start of -1250 marks that earliest secure evidence, not the beginning of domestication.
One proposal holds that wild junglefowl were drawn to rice seeds and nested nearby, and another that chickens were kept first for cockfighting and only later for food; researchers dispute both.

Chickens spread with Austronesian-speaking voyagers across island Southeast Asia, Micronesia, Melanesia, Polynesia and Madagascar, and reached Egypt from the Middle East about 1400 BCE, becoming widely bred there by about 300 BCE.

Whether chickens reached the Americas before European contact is debated: bones from Chile's Arauco Peninsula were dated as pre-Columbian and linked by DNA to Polynesian birds, but further study cast doubt on the result.

More than 26.5 billion chickens were alive in 2023 and more than 50 billion were produced annually for food; about 74 percent of the world's poultry meat and 68 percent of eggs come from factory farming.

A modern broiler may weigh about 1.8 kilograms at 35 days against about 1.05 kilograms for a heritage bird, and the life expectancy of commercial laying hens falls from around seven years to under two.
species/chicken.context: The chicken's early history may be tied to the fields of the Domestication of Rice, it traveled with the Austronesian Expansion and the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific, and it was bred widely by the Ancient Egyptians. It belongs to the wider record of Animal Domestication. The Chicken sits in the Bronze Age and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy, Technology and Earth Systems and Life.
species/chicken.observer: The Observer notes that a bird first kept for reasons we cannot yet fix, food, ritual or sport, has become the largest vertebrate population humans have ever raised, and that its industrial form shows a tool-lineage of breeding and housing that reshapes an animal within a few decades. Many people regard the conditions of industrial flocks as suffering and others weigh them against low food prices, and the Observer records that this disagreement is now part of the chicken's history. The reading would weaken if earlier secure chicken remains are found that change the sequence of its domestication.
questions: When and where were chickens first domesticated, and were they kept first for food, sport or ritual?
Did chickens reach the Americas before 1492?

species/coffee.title: Coffee
species/coffee.summary: Coffee is a shrub whose beans, first documented as a drink among Sufi communities in Yemen by the late 15th century, spread through the Ottoman Empire and Europe and were then grown on slave and colonial plantations across the tropics.
facts: Coffee's popular origin story, in which a 9th-century Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi discovers the plant's effects on his flock, does not appear in writing before 1671 and is likely a later legend; there is no confirmed evidence of coffee as a drink before the 15th century, when it was well established among Sufi communities in Yemen.

The first known coffeehouse opened in Istanbul in 1555, and Pope Clement VIII's declaration of coffee as an acceptable Christian drink in 1600 helped it spread in Catholic Europe; the first European coffeehouse outside Ottoman territory opened in Venice in 1647.

French naval officer Gabriel de Clieu brought coffee plants to Martinique in the 1720s, and cultivation began in the French colony of Saint-Domingue (Haiti) in 1734; by 1788 Saint-Domingue, worked by enslaved laborers, supplied roughly half the world's coffee, and the harsh conditions on its plantations were a contributing factor in the Haitian Revolution.
Coffee reached Brazil in 1727, but large-scale cultivation there did not take off until after independence in 1822.

Coffee cultivation across its colonial-era expansion generally displaced and exploited Indigenous and enslaved populations, a pattern recorded here as sustained harm rather than as an incidental cost of production.
Global coffee production reached about 11 million tonnes in 2023, with Brazil producing about 31 percent and Vietnam the second-largest share.
species/coffee.context: Coffee's early spread from Yemen through the Ottoman Empire followed routes tied to the wider Indian Ocean Trade Network, and its colonial-era plantation economy in the Caribbean is linked to the Atlantic Slave Trade and helped provoke the Haitian Revolution; its global spread after the 16th century belongs to the broader Columbian Exchange of plants and practices between continents. It sits in the Medieval Period and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
species/coffee.observer: The Observer notes that coffee began its documented history bound up with a meaning-engine, used by Sufi communities to stay alert for nighttime devotions, before becoming a secular drink of Ottoman and European coffeehouses that themselves became new sites of conversation and commerce, a shift in the substance's story-glue from devotion to sociability. Its later spread onto slave-worked plantations shows the same plant enabling both a set of religious practices and one of the most extractive labor systems in early modern history, and the Observer treats the suffering on those plantations as inseparable from the substance's global rise. The reading would weaken if the popular Kaldi legend proves to rest on an older oral tradition rather than being a 17th-century invention.
questions: How much of coffee's early diffusion outside Yemen followed Sufi religious networks specifically, as opposed to general trade contacts?
How did the labor conditions on 18th-century coffee plantations compare with those on sugar plantations in the same colonies?

species/cotton.title: Cotton
species/cotton.summary: Cotton was domesticated independently in the Indus Valley of South Asia and in the Americas, and its later mechanized processing in Britain and the American South tied the plant directly to the Industrial Revolution and to the expansion of slavery.
facts: Cotton textile fragments and spindle whorls from Mohenjo-daro in the Indus Valley date to the 3rd millennium BCE, and the date_start of -3000 marks this firmly dated use; mineralized thread at Mehrgarh, dated by some to the 6th millennium BCE, would be earlier but is less certain.

Cotton was domesticated separately in the Americas, with Gossypium hirsutum in Mexico dated to about 3400 to 2300 BCE, bolls from a Tehuacán cave dated to as early as 5500 BCE, and a different species in use in Peru by the 7th to 6th millennia BCE.

Indian cotton textiles, especially from Bengal and Dhaka, were the most important manufactured goods in 18th-century world trade and held about a quarter of the global textile trade, until British colonial tariffs and policy suppressed Indian exports and favored British cloth.

Processing a bale of cotton by hand took over 600 hours of labor until Eli Whitney's gin, patented in 1793, cut that to about a dozen hours; the gin made large-scale growing far more profitable and drove a rapid expansion of slavery in the American South, where cotton was the backbone of the regional economy by the mid-19th century.
India is the largest cotton producer today and the United States has long been the largest exporter; world output is roughly 25 million tonnes a year on about 2.5 percent of the world's arable land.

Cotton needs an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 liters of water per kilogram of fiber worldwide and up to about 22,500 liters in drier regions of India, and conventional growing relies heavily on fertilizers and pesticides, though pest-resistant Bt cotton has cut insecticide use in some regions.
species/cotton.context: Cotton's earliest Old World cultivation is tied to the Indus Valley Civilization, and its colonial-era displacement in favor of British manufacturing became central to the economy of the British Raj. Its mechanized processing fed the Industrial Revolution and the plantation slavery that helped bring on the American Civil War, and the enslaved labor that grew it in the American South is part of the wider Atlantic Slave Trade. Cotton sits in the Bronze Age and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Technology.
species/cotton.observer: The Observer notes that cotton was domesticated independently in at least two hemispheres, so its usefulness was discovered separately and not diffused from one origin, and that a single invention, the gin, turned a labor bottleneck into an incentive to enslave more people, a case where a tool-lineage advance amplified sanctioned harm instead of reducing it. Britain's suppression of Indian manufacturing in favor of its own industry also shows an exchange-web reshaped by state policy to benefit one side. The reading would weaken if the gin's role in expanding slavery proves small relative to rising cotton prices and available land.
questions: How independent were the Old World and American domestications of cotton, and did any early contact or diffusion occur between them?
How much of the decline of Indian cotton manufacturing reflects deliberate colonial policy as opposed to British industrial efficiency alone?

species/cyanobacteria.title: Cyanobacteria
species/cyanobacteria.summary: Cyanobacteria are bacteria that perform oxygen-producing photosynthesis. Their activity led to the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere.
facts: The earliest unambiguous cyanobacterial fossils are about 2.15 billion years old, and direct fossil evidence of photosynthetic membranes is about 1.75 billion years old. Biomarker evidence once cited for 2.7 billion years was later shown to be younger contamination, so the 2.7-billion-year start date used for this note reflects an older, disputed estimate and is approximate.
Chloroplasts in plants and algae descend from cyanobacteria through endosymbiosis.
They still live in oceans, lakes, and soils around the world.
The Great Oxidation Event followed their spread.
species/cyanobacteria.context: Cyanobacteria are the biological agents of the Great Oxidation Event, which reshaped the planet's chemistry in the Proterozoic Eon.
species/cyanobacteria.observer: The Observer regards them as the earlier example of a species that changed the atmosphere. Their oxygen was a byproduct, not a goal.
questions: When did oxygen-producing photosynthesis first evolve?

species/denisovans.title: Denisovans
species/denisovans.summary: Denisovans are an extinct human group known first from DNA in a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2010.
facts: Very few fossils are known, including a jaw from Xiahe in Tibet.
Some living populations, especially in Oceania and East Asia, carry Denisovan DNA.
A gene variant helping Tibetans adapt to high altitude came from Denisovans.

The Harbin cranium (at least 146,000 years old, once nicknamed 'Dragon Man' and named Homo longi) was linked to Denisovans in 2025, using mitochondrial DNA recovered from dental calculus and ancient protein evidence, in studies published in Cell and Science. It is the first Denisovan skull identified.
species/denisovans.context: Denisovans are close relatives of Homo neanderthalensis and interbred with Homo sapiens during the Out of Africa Dispersal.
species/denisovans.observer: The Observer notes a species identified mostly from its DNA, before its appearance was known. The molecular record now reveals populations that fossils alone did not.
questions: What did Denisovans look like, and how widely did they live?

species/dinosaurs.title: Dinosaurs
species/dinosaurs.summary: Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles that dominated land ecosystems for about 165 million years. Birds are living descendants of one dinosaur lineage.
facts: The earliest dinosaurs appeared roughly 233 million years ago in the Triassic.
Non-avian dinosaurs ranged from chicken-sized to the largest land animals ever.
Many had feathers, and birds descend from small feathered theropods.
Non-avian dinosaurs died out in the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction.
species/dinosaurs.context: Dinosaurs define the Mesozoic Era. They rose after the Triassic-Jurassic Extinction and ended with the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction.
species/dinosaurs.observer: The Observer notes that dinosaurs are still with us as birds. Extinction is not always total, and lineages can continue in other forms.
questions: How did dinosaur physiology work?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: First dinosaurs about 243-233 Ma in the Triassic [English Wikipedia]

species/domestic-cat.title: Domestic Cat
species/domestic-cat.summary: The domestic cat descends from the African wildcat and was first tamed in the Near East by Neolithic farmers, with the earliest evidence of a tamed wildcat buried near a human grave on Cyprus about 7500 to 7200 BCE.
facts: Domestic cats descend from the African wildcat (Felis lybica), and the earliest known sign of a tamed wildcat is a burial found close to a human Neolithic grave at Shillourokambos, southern Cyprus, dated to about 7500 to 7200 BCE.

The leading explanation is that African wildcats were drawn to early farming settlements in the Fertile Crescent by rodents, especially the house mouse, and were tolerated and then tamed, a long relationship that lasted thousands of years.
Cats were venerated in Egypt from about 3100 BCE, and Egyptian wildcats later contributed to the maternal gene pool of the domestic cat.
As farming spread, so did cats: they reached Greece about 1200 BCE with traders, southern Europe by the 5th century BCE and northern Germany by the 5th century CE.

In the United States alone domestic cats are estimated to kill 1.3 to 4.0 billion birds and 6.3 to 22.3 billion mammals a year, and abandoned pets add to a global feral cat population that has driven declines of bird, mammal and reptile species.
species/domestic-cat.context: Cats entered human settlements through the storage of Wheat and Barley in The Agricultural Revolution, and their veneration by the Ancient Egyptians is a well-known case of a domesticated animal treated as sacred. Cats belong to the wider record of Animal Domestication. The Domestic Cat sits in the Neolithic and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief and Earth Systems and Life.
species/domestic-cat.observer: The Observer offers a reading, not a fact: the cat is the strongest case for the idea that an animal may have chosen the arrangement more than humans did, since a hunter of grain-store rodents needed no training and asked only to be left alone, so the phrase "who domesticated whom" fits here better than for most species. The same animal was honored in Egyptian ritual and now, in large numbers outdoors, is a predator of wild birds and small mammals, a reminder that a meaning-engine's favorite creature can also be an ecological actor. The reading would weaken if the Cyprus burial proves to be an isolated taming with no descendants among modern cats.
questions: Did cats spread from a single Near Eastern source, or did more than one wildcat population contribute to the domestic cat?
How did the veneration of cats in Egypt affect the movement of cats across the Mediterranean?

species/domestic-pig.title: Domestic Pig
species/domestic-pig.summary: The domestic pig was bred from the wild boar in the Near East, in or around the Tigris basin, by about 9400 BCE, was domesticated again independently in China, and is now tied with chicken as the most commonly eaten meat in the world.
facts: Domestic pigs descend from the wild boar (Sus scrofa) and were first domesticated in the Near East, in or around the Tigris basin; pigs brought to Cyprus more than 11,400 years ago imply domestication or close management on the mainland by then.
Pigs were domesticated separately in China starting some 8,000 years ago.

Pigs reached Europe at least 8,500 years ago and over the next 3,000 years interbred with European wild boar until their genomes held less than 5 percent Near Eastern ancestry, a change that amounts to a further, local domestication.
Austronesian-speaking peoples carried pigs across island Southeast Asia and Oceania beginning about 4,000 years ago, and most pigs from the Philippines to Hawai‘i descend from those introductions.

Spanish explorers including Hernando de Soto brought pigs to southeastern North America, where escaped animals became feral; feral pigs now damage crops and wildlife in the United States, New Zealand, northern Queensland and South America.
Eating pork is forbidden in Islam and Judaism, and pigs are sacred in some other religions.
About 850 million pigs were alive in 2019, with China holding about 36.5 percent, and roughly 1.5 billion are slaughtered each year.
species/domestic-pig.context: Pigs were among the animals brought under Animal Domestication as part of The Agricultural Revolution, they crossed the Pacific with the Austronesian Expansion and the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific, and they reached the Americas through the Columbian Exchange. The Domestic Pig sits in the Neolithic and the region Mesopotamia, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
species/domestic-pig.observer: The Observer notes that the pig is at once one of the most eaten animals and one of the most avoided, so a single food can work as a claim-line drawn at the table between communities; the origins of the prohibitions are debated, and the Observer does not choose among the explanations. Pigs also travel well, since they eat almost anything and breed quickly, which made them useful cargo for Austronesian voyagers and Spanish ships, an exchange-web carrying a whole food supply across oceans. The reading would weaken if the prohibitions prove to have had little to do with marking group boundaries.
questions: Where and when were pigs first domesticated in the Near East, given that the Cyprus evidence points to an earlier date than most mainland finds?
How did the replacement of Near Eastern pig lineages in Europe unfold, and did local people domesticate wild boar on their own?

species/donkey.title: Donkey
species/donkey.summary: The donkey was domesticated from the African wild ass in northeastern Africa, probably by pastoralists in Nubia, some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, and became the main pack animal of early long-distance trade in Egypt and Southwest Asia.
facts: Donkeys descend from the African wild ass (Equus africanus) and were domesticated in Africa some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, probably by pastoral people in Nubia; remains from the fourth millennium BCE have been found at Ma'adi in Lower Egypt, and the date_start of -4000 is the midpoint of that range.

Donkeys were vital to long-distance trade in Egypt, and in the Fourth Dynasty (about 2675 to 2565 BCE) wealthy individuals were known to own more than 1,000 of them, used as pack animals and in farming and for milk and meat.

By the end of the fourth millennium BCE donkeys had spread to Southwest Asia, the main breeding center had shifted to Mesopotamia by about 1800 BCE, and the Greeks and Romans later spread them through their empires.
A male donkey crossed with a female horse produces a mule, and the reverse cross produces a hinny; mules are valued as working and riding animals in many countries.
More than 40 million donkeys were alive in the early 2000s, about 96 percent of them in developing countries, where they are used mainly as pack animals or for draught work.
species/donkey.context: Donkeys served the trade networks of the Ancient Egyptians and were probably first kept by pastoralists in Nubia, the region later home to the Kingdom of Kush, before the Horse and the Dromedary and Bactrian Camels took over much of the long-distance carrying. They are part of Animal Domestication. The Donkey sits in the Neolithic and the region Nile Valley, and belongs to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Technology.
species/donkey.observer: The Observer notes that the animal which made early caravans possible is seldom the one honored in a society's story-glue, since chariots and cavalry receive the poems and the donkey carried the grain, copper and cloth; the record is therefore weighted toward what humans admired, not what they relied on. Owning a thousand donkeys was a status-signal in the Fourth Dynasty, which suggests that carrying capacity was itself a form of wealth. The reading would weaken if excavated caravan and settlement records show that horses or camels carried more early long-distance cargo than donkeys did.
questions: Was the donkey domesticated once or several times, and where exactly did the process begin?
How large was the donkey trade between Egypt and neighboring regions during the third millennium BCE?

species/dromedary-and-bactrian-camels.title: Dromedary and Bactrian Camels
species/dromedary-and-bactrian-camels.summary: Two camel species were domesticated by about the middle of the third millennium BCE, the one-humped dromedary in southern Arabia or Somalia and the two-humped Bactrian camel in Central Asia, and together they made long-distance caravan travel across deserts possible.
facts: The dromedary was domesticated in Somalia or southern Arabia during the third millennium BCE, though a 2016 genetic study points to southeastern Arabia.

The Bactrian camel was domesticated in Central Asia around 2500 BCE, with evidence at Shahr-e Sukhteh in Iran, and one analysis places its domestication east of the Zagros Mountains by the middle of the third millennium BCE.
The military Arabian saddle developed in the 7th century BCE, and between about 500 and 100 BCE Bactrian camels entered military use with new saddles placed over the humps.

About 14 million camels were alive in 2010, roughly 90 percent of them dromedaries; the domestic Bactrian numbers about 1.4 million, and the wild Bactrian, a separate species, is reduced to about 1,000 animals and is still declining.
Frankincense and myrrh moved from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa to Mediterranean and Mesopotamian markets mostly by camel caravan, for well over a thousand years.
More than a million dromedaries are estimated to be feral in Australia, a population growing by about 8 percent a year that stood at about 700,000 in 2008.
species/dromedary-and-bactrian-camels.context: Camels made the desert routes of the Incense Trade work, linking the Kingdom of Saba and the Nabataeans to Mediterranean and Mesopotamian markets, and Bactrian camels served the overland routes that became the Opening of the Silk Roads. Both species are part of Animal Domestication. The camels sit in the Bronze Age and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belong to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
species/dromedary-and-bactrian-camels.observer: The Observer notes that camels changed what counted as an obstacle: a desert that stopped other animals became a road that only certain traders could use, so the people who held wells and caravan stops held a claim-line over the flow of goods, and cities such as those of Saba and the Nabataeans grew on that control. A saddle is a small tool-lineage change, yet the Arabian and Bactrian saddles turned a pack animal into a war animal within a few centuries. The reading would weaken if the routes proved to have been used mainly for local exchange rather than long-distance trade.
questions: Where exactly was the dromedary first domesticated, and how did it reach North Africa?
How much did the saddle innovations change the volume of trade across the deserts?

species/dunkleosteus.title: Dunkleosteus
species/dunkleosteus.summary: Dunkleosteus was a large armored placoderm fish of the Late Devonian with bony blades in place of teeth. Its best-known species, D. terrelli, comes from the Cleveland Shale of Ohio; its size has been revised downward and its bite force is under review.
facts: The genus is reported from the Late Devonian, about 382 to 359 million years ago, but D. terrelli is best documented from about 372 to 360 million years ago, chiefly in the Cleveland Shale of Ohio. Ten species have been named, and about four are widely accepted.

Older reconstructions gave lengths of 6 to 10 m. A 2023 study using the eye socket and cheek plate estimated about 3.4 m for typical adults and about 4.1 m for the largest. It has not been independently replicated.

A 2007 study modeled the skull as a linked lever system and estimated a bite force of about 4,400 newtons at the tip and 5,400 at the blade edge, for an individual then thought to be 6 m long. A 2025 study argues that these figures need re-examination.
The name was coined in 1956 by Jean-Pierre Lehman to honor David Dunkle. Placoderms died out at the end-Devonian Hangenberg event, about 359 million years ago.
species/dunkleosteus.context: Dunkleosteus lived in the Devonian Period, the Age of Fishes, alongside lobe-finned relatives of Tiktaalik during the Fish-to-Tetrapod Transition. Placoderms declined in the Late Devonian Extinction. Compare the arthropod predators, Eurypterids. See Earth Systems and Life and Science.
species/dunkleosteus.observer: The Observer notes that the animal long shown as the great predator of its age shrank by about half on re-measurement, the ordinary condition of deep-time knowledge, in which a confident number is a reading of a few skulls. A whole class of armored fishes left no descendants while a lobe-finned relative went on to land, and nothing in the record marked which would. The reading would weaken if independent studies reproduced the older, larger sizes.
questions: How large did Dunkleosteus grow, and how hard could it bite?
Which of the named species are valid?

species/ediacaran-biota.title: Ediacaran Biota
species/ediacaran-biota.summary: The Ediacaran biota are the first large, complex, multicellular organisms in the fossil record, living in the sea in the last stretch of the Proterozoic, before the Cambrian.
facts: The Ediacaran Period spans about 635 to 538.8 million years ago.
The biota are named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia and are known also from Newfoundland, Namibia, and the White Sea coast of Russia.
Many forms were soft-bodied and frond-, disc-, or quilt-shaped.
The relationship of many Ediacaran forms to living animal groups is unclear.
The classic assemblages largely disappear near the start of the Cambrian.
species/ediacaran-biota.context: The Ediacaran biota follow the glaciations of Snowball Earth and precede the Cambrian Explosion. They belong to the Proterozoic Eon. Ediacaran Biota sits in the Proterozoic Eon and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
species/ediacaran-biota.observer: The Observer notes that Earth ran a large-bodied experiment in multicellular life that left no obvious descendants. Continuity is not guaranteed: some lineages simply end. This reading would be undermined if most Ediacaran forms were shown to be ancestral to living animals.
questions: Which Ediacaran forms, if any, were true animals?
What ended the assemblage: extinction, competition, or changing chemistry?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: The Ediacara fauna is named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, and one of the oldest dated assemblages of Ediacaran organisms, in the Avalon Zone of Newfoundland, has an age of 565 million years [Britannica on the Ediacaran Period]

species/eurypterids.title: Eurypterids
species/eurypterids.summary: Eurypterids, or sea scorpions, were predatory arthropods that lived from the Ordovician to the Permian, about 467 to 252 million years ago. They were relatives of spiders and horseshoe crabs, not true scorpions, and included one of the largest arthropods known, about 2.5 m in body length.
facts: The oldest well-described eurypterid, Pentecopterus from Iowa, is about 467 to 458 million years old. Moroccan fragments reported in 2025 may be about 479 million years old but are tentatively assigned.
All eurypterids are chelicerates, the group of spiders, scorpions, and horseshoe crabs. A 2013 analysis placed them closer to arachnids than to horseshoe crabs, which remains debated.

The largest, Jaekelopterus rhenaniae of the Early Devonian of Germany, was estimated in 2007 from a pincer fragment to have a pincer about 46 cm long and a body about 2.5 m long, without the extended pincers. Another study argued for a smaller size.

Only the earliest eurypterids were strictly marine; many later forms lived in brackish or fresh water. A 6-m trackway in Carboniferous sandstone in Scotland has been attributed to a land-walking Hibbertopterus, an inference.
After the Late Devonian extinction only three families reached the Carboniferous and Permian. The last records are Permian, about 254 to 252 million years old at the latest.
species/eurypterids.context: Eurypterids arose during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification beside Trilobites, flourished in the Silurian Period and Devonian Period, declined in the Late Devonian Extinction, and were gone by the Permian-Triassic Extinction. Compare the armored fish Dunkleosteus. See Earth Systems and Life and Colonization of Land.
species/eurypterids.observer: The Observer notes that one of the largest arthropods ever to live belonged to a group now known chiefly to specialists, and that its size is scaled from a fragment of claw. A lineage that lasted about 215 million years and left no descendants shows that persistence does not guarantee survival. The reading would weaken if eurypterids proved to have been displaced by competitors, not by environmental change.
questions: When did the last eurypterids die out?
How large did Jaekelopterus grow?

species/flowering-plants.title: Flowering Plants
species/flowering-plants.summary: Flowering plants (angiosperms) appear in the fossil record in the Early Cretaceous, about 130 million years ago, and now make up most land plant species.
facts: The oldest widely accepted angiosperm pollen dates to the Hauterivian and Barremian ages of the Early Cretaceous, about 133 to 125 million years ago.
The oldest well-preserved flowering-plant macrofossils, such as those from China, date to about 125 million years ago.
Some molecular-clock studies place their origin earlier, in the Triassic or Jurassic; this gap is debated.
Flowering plants radiated rapidly in the Cretaceous alongside pollinating insects.
Cereals, legumes, fruits, and most other crops descend from this group.
species/flowering-plants.context: Flowering plants diversified in the age of the Dinosaurs and survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction. Every crop of The Agricultural Revolution belongs to this lineage. Flowering Plants sits in the Mesozoic Era and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
species/flowering-plants.observer: The Observer notes that the species' whole agricultural existence rests on one plant lineage that evolved to attract animals into carrying its pollen and seeds. Farming can be read as the species joining a partnership that plants had run with insects for more than a hundred million years.
questions: Why was the origin of flowering plants so abrupt in the fossil record?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: Fossil angiosperm pollen is found in the Hauterivian and Barremian ages, about 132.9 to 125 million years ago, though angiosperm-like pollen found in Switzerland in 2013 dates to the Middle Triassic (about 247.2 to 242 million years ago); Archaefructus from the Yixian Formation of China is dated to about 125 million years ago; molecular clocks give older origins [Britannica on Angiosperm Paleobotany and Evolution; Britannica on Archaefructus; Nature Communications 2025 Angiosperm Crown Age]

species/goat.title: Goat
species/goat.summary: The domestic goat was bred from the wild bezoar ibex in southwestern Asia around 10,000 years ago, one of the first animals kept by farming communities, and it remains valued today for milk, meat and fiber, especially on marginal land unsuited to other livestock.
facts: Domestic goats descend from the bezoar ibex, a wild goat still found in the Zagros Mountains of Iran and formerly widespread in Anatolia, and domestication is dated to about 10,000 years ago in Southwest Asia and Eastern Europe.

The earliest clear archaeological evidence for goat domestication comes from Ganj Dareh in Iran, with further early sites at Jericho, Choga Mami, Djeitun and Çayönü dating domestication to between about 8,000 and 9,000 years ago.
Neolithic herders used goats for milk and meat and also made use of their dung as fuel and their bones, hair and sinew for tools, building materials and clothing.

Goats remain economically important today for dairy, providing about 2 percent of the world's total annual milk supply, and for fiber such as cashmere and mohair, valued in part for their hardiness on land too marginal for cattle or sheep.

More than 1.1 billion goats were living worldwide as of 2022, of which about 150 million were in India, the largest single-country population; India was also the largest goat-milk producer that year, followed by Bangladesh and South Sudan.
species/goat.context: Goats were among the earliest animals brought under Animal Domestication, a pillar of The Agricultural Revolution in the Fertile Crescent alongside Sheep, domesticated in a similar place and period and often herded together. Goats sit in the Neolithic and the region Iranian Plateau, and belong to the theme threads of Trade and Economy and Technology.
species/goat.observer: The Observer offers a reading, not a fact: that the goat's continuing importance on land too poor for cattle or sheep suggests its domestication gave early farming communities a way to draw food and materials from marginal ground that would otherwise have supported no livestock at all, extending the reach of the Settling into harsher terrain. That goats and sheep were domesticated in the same general region and period, and are still often herded together, points to an early kin-lattice of pastoral practice that treated the two species as complementary rather than as competitors for the same land. The reading would weaken if goat and sheep domestication are shown to have occurred at meaningfully different times or in different communities rather than in close succession.
questions: How closely linked were the domestication of goats and sheep, and did one community likely tame both, or did the practices spread separately?
How has goat herding on marginal land changed as climate change alters which regions count as marginal?

species/hallucigenia.title: Hallucigenia
species/hallucigenia.summary: Hallucigenia is a small, worm-like Cambrian animal with paired back spines and clawed legs, known from the Burgess Shale of Canada and from China, about 510 to 505 million years ago. It is known for being reconstructed upside down in 1977 and for the 2015 discovery of its head.
facts: Three species are named: H. sparsa from the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, H. fortis from Chengjiang and H. hongmeia from Guanshan, both in Yunnan, China. The Burgess Shale is about 505 million years old by fossil zones; Chengjiang is at most 518.
H. sparsa is about 3 cm long, though published maxima reach 5.5 cm, and it is rare, about 0.19 percent of specimens counted in the Walcott Quarry.

In 1977 Simon Conway Morris reconstructed it walking on stilt-like spines with tentacles along its back. Work on Chinese specimens in 1991 showed that the spines were on top and the "tentacles" were legs.
In 2015 Martin Smith and Jean-Bernard Caron showed that the supposed head was a decay stain. The true head has a pair of simple eyes, a mouth ringed with plates, and a toothed throat.
Its claws resemble those of living velvet worms, and it is placed among the lobopodians, stem relatives of that group. Some analyses place it more basally among the panarthropods.
species/hallucigenia.context: Hallucigenia lived in the Cambrian Period, during and after the Cambrian Explosion, and shared the Burgess Shale with Anomalocaris and Pikaia. At Chengjiang Fossil Site it lived alongside Trilobites. See Earth Systems and Life and Science.
species/hallucigenia.observer: The Observer notes that an animal a few centimeters long was drawn upside down for fourteen years and its head found only in 2015. Much of the deep past is a reading of evidence, and the reading changes when specimens arrive. The reading would weaken if later study showed the 2015 head identification to be mistaken.
questions: Where does Hallucigenia sit among the panarthropods?
How many valid species does the genus contain?

species/homo-erectus.title: Homo erectus
species/homo-erectus.summary: Homo erectus was an early human species that lived from about 1.9 million to roughly 110,000 years ago, the first known hominin to spread widely beyond Africa.
facts: Fossils have been found in Africa, Georgia (Dmanisi, about 1.8 million years old), and East and Southeast Asia.
It made Acheulean handaxes and probably used fire; see Control of Fire.
Its brain was about 900 cubic centimeters and its body proportions were similar to modern humans'.
It may be the longest-lived human species.
species/homo-erectus.context: H. erectus is ancestral or related to later Homo species, including Homo sapiens. See Pleistocene Epoch.
species/homo-erectus.observer: The Observer notes that a species survived for well over a million years with much the same toolkit. Human history's rapid pace is recent.
questions: Which later species descended from H. erectus?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Average brain about 900 cc; Dmanisi fossils about 1.8 Ma [Smithsonian Human Origins Program]

species/homo-floresiensis.title: Homo floresiensis
species/homo-floresiensis.summary: Homo floresiensis, nicknamed 'the hobbit', was a small-bodied human species that lived on the Indonesian island of Flores. Its bones date to about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, and stone tools attributed to it extend to about 50,000 years ago.
facts: It was discovered in 2003 at Liang Bua Cave.
Adults stood about 1.1 meters tall, with a brain of about 400 cubic centimeters.
It made stone tools and lived on an island isolated by deep water.
Whether it descended from H. erectus or an earlier ancestor is debated.
species/homo-floresiensis.context: H. floresiensis shows that several human species overlapped in time with Homo sapiens. See Homo erectus.
species/homo-floresiensis.observer: The Observer notes that isolated islands can produce unexpected forms. For most of the Pleistocene, the species was not alone.
questions: What was its ancestry?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Remains dated 100-60 ka; associated stone tools 190-50 ka [Sutikna et al. 2016 Homo floresiensis Chronology]

species/homo-habilis.title: Homo habilis
species/homo-habilis.summary: Homo habilis ('handy man') is an early member of the genus Homo that lived in Africa from about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago.
facts: It was named in 1964 from fossils at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania.
Its brain was roughly 500 to 700 cubic centimeters (estimates vary).
It is associated with Oldowan Stone Tools, though the link is not certain.
Whether it is a distinct species or a variant of other early Homo is debated.
species/homo-habilis.context: H. habilis appears in the Pleistocene Epoch and precedes Homo erectus.
species/homo-habilis.observer: The Observer notes that the label 'human' was pushed back in time by each new discovery. The boundary of the genus is blurred.
questions: What is the relationship of H. habilis to other early Homo?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Named 1964 from Olduvai; lived about 2.3-1.5 (or 2.4-1.4) Ma [Smithsonian Human Origins Program]

species/homo-naledi.title: Homo naledi
species/homo-naledi.summary: Homo naledi is a small-brained human relative whose remains were found in the Rising Star cave system in South Africa in 2013, dated to about 335,000 to 236,000 years ago.
facts: Fossils of at least 15 individuals were found deep in a cave.
The brain size was about 500 cubic centimeters, yet the species lived at the same time as early Homo sapiens.
Researchers have proposed deliberate burial and cave markings, but those claims are contested.
Its combination of primitive and modern features is unusual.
species/homo-naledi.context: H. naledi lived in the same time and continent as early Homo sapiens and challenges the link between large brains and complex behavior.
species/homo-naledi.observer: The Observer notes that if the burial claims hold, complex treatment of the dead would not require a large brain. The claim is under active debate.
questions: Did H. naledi bury its dead?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Fossils dated to about 236,000 to 335,000 years ago [Dirks et al. 2017 Homo naledi Age]

species/homo-neanderthalensis.title: Homo neanderthalensis
species/homo-neanderthalensis.summary: Neanderthals were a human species that lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to about 40,000 years ago and interbred with Homo sapiens.
facts: They had large brains, robust bodies adapted to cold, and made Mousterian stone tools.
The Neanderthal genome was first sequenced in 2010.
Non-African people today derive up to about 2 percent of their ancestry from Neanderthals.
Evidence for burial, ornaments, and pigment use is debated but growing.
species/homo-neanderthalensis.context: Neanderthals met Homo sapiens during the Out of Africa Dispersal. Compare Denisovans.
species/homo-neanderthalensis.observer: The Observer notes that Neanderthals are not a separate story: they live on in the DNA of most of the species. The line between species was permeable.
questions: Why did Neanderthals disappear?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: A draft Neandertal genome was first published in Science on 7 May 2010; some present-day humans derive about 2 percent of their ancestry from Neanderthals [Green et al. 2010 Neandertal Genome; Sankararaman et al. 2016 Neanderthal and Denisovan Ancestry Map]

species/homo-sapiens.title: Homo sapiens
species/homo-sapiens.summary: Homo sapiens is the species of modern humans: the only living member of the genus Homo, which emerged in Africa about 300,000 years ago and now numbers about eight billion.
facts: Modern humans have a brain of about 1,350 cubic centimeters.
They are notable for language, symbolic thought, and cumulative culture.
They have inhabited every continent and now live in cities, deserts, polar stations, and orbit.
Genetic diversity is relatively low compared with other apes.
species/homo-sapiens.context: See Origin of Homo sapiens and Out of Africa Dispersal. This species is the subject of the Observer's inquiry; see Observer's Charter.
species/homo-sapiens.observer: The Observer's subject: a species that is defined less by a single trait than by a combination, including cumulative learning, large-scale cooperation, and an unusual dependence on shared stories.
questions: What best explains the species' rapid cultural change?
